questions.q: Define marketing in one sentence using the Philip Kotler definition. Include the phrases "social process" and "freely exchanging."
questions.a: Correct answer: Marketing is a social process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering, and freely exchanging products and services of value with others. A wrong answer that says "marketing is selling products" or "marketing is advertising" reveals the student equates marketing with only promotion or transaction, missing the need-identification, value-creation, and relationship-building dimensions.

questions.q: A student says: "Marketing and selling are the same thing — both are about getting rid of what the factory makes." Explain why this statement is incorrect using the concepts of 'starting point' and 'focus'.
questions.a: Correct explanation: Selling starts with the factory's existing output and focuses on converting products into cash through persuasion (seller's needs). Marketing starts with identifying customer needs and focuses on creating value that satisfies those needs profitably (buyer's needs). A wrong answer that only mentions "selling is part of marketing" without contrasting the starting point and focus shows the student has not grasped the fundamental philosophical difference — a classic board exam trap.

questions.q: A local bakery wants to expand its business. The owner currently only sells walk-in cakes. List THREE new entities from the scope of marketing (beyond 'goods') that the bakery could market, and give a specific example for each.
questions.a: Correct answer (any three with valid examples): Services — custom cake decorating workshops; Experiences — "bake your own bread" weekend sessions; Events — hosting a "Monsoon Cupcake Festival"; Persons — marketing the head baker as a celebrity chef for corporate demos; Places — promoting the bakery as a heritage food-tour stop; Properties — franchising the bakery brand/recipes; Organizations — partnering with a coffee chain for co-branded outlets; Information — selling a paid recipe e-book; Ideas — promoting "healthy indulgence" or "zero-waste baking" as a lifestyle concept. A wrong answer that lists only "cakes, pastries, bread" (all goods) shows the student cannot extend the scope beyond tangible products.

questions.q: Compare the AMA (2017) definition of marketing with the Kotler definition. Identify ONE key similarity and ONE key difference in their emphasis.
questions.a: (1) Similarity — both treat marketing as a process of creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that carry value, (2) Difference — the AMA definition explicitly adds relationship management that benefits the organisation and its stakeholders, while Kotler stresses the social process of free exchange, (3) Takeaway — relationship management versus voluntary societal exchange is the emphasis gap. A wrong answer saying the two are the same, or citing only the stakeholder clause without the process similarity, shows a superficial reading of the definitions.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "A non-profit organization running a blood donation drive does not need marketing because it is not selling anything." Defend your position using the scope of marketing and the definition of exchange.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The claim is false. The blood donation drive markets an 'idea' (voluntary donation saves lives) and a 'service' (safe, convenient donation process). Exchange occurs: donors give blood (value) and receive psychological satisfaction, a health check-up, and social recognition (value in return). Marketing is needed to identify donor motivations, communicate effectively, reduce fear (product design), choose convenient locations (place), and build long-term donor relationships. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim reveals the misconception that marketing requires monetary transaction or profit motive.

questions.q: Create a new real-world example (not from textbook) of an entity being marketed that fits the 'properties' category in the scope of marketing. Describe the marketer, the target audience, and the value exchanged.
questions.a: Good answer example: A fintech startup (marketer) licenses its proprietary credit-scoring algorithm (property — intellectual property) to regional cooperative banks (target audience). Value exchanged: the startup receives licensing fees and data-network effects; the banks get a tested, regulatory-compliant scoring model without R&D cost. A poor answer that gives "selling a house" (real estate is a good, not a property in the marketing scope sense) or "selling a patent" without explaining the ongoing value exchange shows confusion between legal property rights and the marketing entity category 'properties' (which includes intangible rights like patents, trademarks, franchises, licenses).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Marketing is a social and managerial process by which ______ and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering, and freely exchanging products and services of value with others.

Fill in the blank: You see an Instagram reel reviewing the camera, read a ______ article on a tech website, visit a store to hold the phone, check exchange offers on Amazon, and finally buy it with a bank cashback offer.
What is Marketing? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Marketing is a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering, and freely exchanging products and services of value with others.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Marketing?
questions.a: Students consistently equate marketing with only advertising or selling.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) state at least two standard definitions of marketing (Kotler and AMA) using correct terminology, (2) list and give a real-world example for all 10 entities in the scope of marketing (goods, services, experiences, events, persons, places, properties, organizations, information, ideas), and (3) explain in their own.
